implementation_notes: std's channels are deliberately point-to-point - mpsc delivers each value to a single receiver - so fan-out comes from a runtime or crate: tokio::sync::broadcast is a multi-producer, multi-consumer broadcast queue in which each sent value is seen by all consumers and is stored once, cloned on demand per receiver. Sender::subscribe() adds a subscriber at runtime, which is exactly the registry the pattern describes, and the bounded capacity is the overflow contract: a receiver that falls behind gets RecvError::Lagged instead of unbounded memory growth. Without tokio, a Mutex<Vec<Sender<T>>> or a watch channel (latest value only) are the manual approximations.
pitfalls: send() returns SendError once every receiver has been dropped, so a publish with no subscribers is an error rather than a no-op; decide whether the publisher treats that as failure.
A slow receiver does not block the publisher: the ring buffer overwrites the oldest values and the laggard observes Lagged(n); ignoring that error silently loses messages.

The channel retains each value until every receiver has seen a clone, so a receiver that is never drained pins memory up to the configured capacity; dropping the receiver marks its unread messages as read.
